<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</ol></li>

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">João Cardoso
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Instituto Superior Técnico
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>INESC-ID
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Arlindo L. Oliveira
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Instituto Superior Técnico
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>INESC-ID
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Bruno Martins
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Instituto Superior Técnico
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>INESC-ID
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:joao.n.m.cardoso@tecnico.ulisboa.pt">joao.n.m.cardoso@tecnico.ulisboa.pt</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Understanding what features are encoded by learned directions in LLM activation space requires identifying inputs that strongly activate them. Feature visualization, which optimizes inputs to maximally activate a target direction, offers an alternative to costly dataset search approaches, but remains underexplored for LLMs due to the discrete nature of text. Furthermore, existing prompt optimization techniques are poorly suited to this domain, which is highly prone to local minima. To overcome these limitations, we introduce ADAPT, a hybrid method combining beam search initialization with adaptive gradient-guided mutation, designed around these failure modes. We evaluate on Sparse Autoencoder latents from Gemma 2 2B, proposing metrics grounded in dataset activation statistics to enable rigorous comparison, and show that ADAPT consistently outperforms prior methods across layers and latent types. Our results establish that feature visualization for LLMs is tractable, but requires design assumptions tailored to the domain.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Neural networks construct rich representations of their inputs, often assigned to linear directions in their latent activation space. Understanding the relevant input features encoded by these directions is essential for interpretability efforts, but identifying the range of input patterns that activate a given latent direction (henceforth, <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">latent</span>) is a challenging task. The standard approach is to perform a dataset search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paulo et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bills et al., 2023</a>)</cite>: running the model on a large corpus and registering what input examples maximally activate the directions of interest, which is an effective approach for large-scale surveys where the large computational costs of running a model on a large corpus can be amortized over thousands of latents in parallel. Dataset search is often performed for latent directions learned by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sharkey et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bricken et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, which are designed to yield large dictionaries of interpretable and monosemantic latents. However, with alternate techniques for obtaining latents of interest or more complex sub-components such as model circuits or collections of latents, this approach becomes computationally prohibitive.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">An alternate approach is feature visualization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olah et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, which consists of creating an input that is “tailor-made” for a given latent, via prompt optimization techniques which seek to maximally activate the target latent. This brings several advantages over dataset search:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Overcoming dataset limitations:</span> searched datasets are typically smaller than the model’s training dataset, limiting the number of illustrative examples for any given latent.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Disentangling correlated features:</span> if two features happen to be correlated in the searched dataset (e.g. a semantic concept and the language of the text), it is hard to tease apart the latent’s corresponding feature. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olah et al., 2017</a>)</cite></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Versatility:</span> any feature optimization can be modified to incorporate complex objectives and penalties.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Causal grounding:</span> Correlational methods can produce plausible-looking explanations even for randomly initialized networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Méloux et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Feature visualization constructs inputs that cause activation, sidestepping spurious associations in any fixed corpus.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These advantages are visible in previous vision interpretability work, which has made extensive use of feature visualization. However, the application of these techniques to LLMs has been limited, mostly due to the discrete nature of textual inputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thompson et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which precludes direct gradient-based updates. In this work, we take inspiration from existing adversarial prompt optimization techniques, where the objective is to induce the model to generate outputs that bypass its safety training, and from previous LLM feature visualization work. Our contributions are as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce ADAPT, a new algorithm that outperforms existing baselines by combining beam-search initialization with gradient-guided mutation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate ADAPT and previous methods on SAE latents from Gemma 2 2B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemma Team, 2024</a>)</cite>, introducing metrics grounded in dataset activation statistics to enable systematic comparison of different techniques.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the reliability of gradient-based optimization methods for this application domain, and investigate the role of fluency penalties in prompt optimization for feature visualization.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Background ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> covers background on SAEs and existing prompt optimization methods. Section <a href="#S3" title="3 ADAPT: Adaptive DynAmic Prompt Tuning ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> introduces ADAPT. Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> presents our experimental evaluation, followed by an analysis of the common failure modes of several existing methods. In section <a href="#S5" title="5 Extensions ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> we extend ADAPT to a dual latent objective, to illustrate its versatility. We conclude in Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Conclusions ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We review sparse autoencoders, which provide our evaluation testbed, and existing prompt optimization methods, whose limitations motivate ADAPT.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Sparse autoencoders</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The representation vectors constructed by LLMs are thought to contain far more features than they have dimensions, by encoding them as non-orthogonal directions in activation space that do not align with the neuronal basis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elhage et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) learn to reconstruct a target representation vector through a high-dimension middle layer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bricken et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Templeton et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. A sparsity penalty encourages most latent dimensions to remain inactive after the activation function, yielding a small set of active directions that capture the input vector’s variability. These directions have been shown to be more monosemantic, in the sense of being correlated with single input features, than individual neurons.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While the proposed ADAPT method can accommodate arbitrary directions or complex objectives, we focus on SAE latents due to the availability of open source tools that support the development of our technique, by mitigating the need to retrieve target latents ourselves, and by enabling comparison with existing latent interpretation techniques, namely dataset search, without incurring in high computational costs. In particular, the Gemma Scope project <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lieberum et al., 2024</a>)</cite> has made publicly available a suite of SAEs, with additional latent statistics and dataset examples provided via the Neuronpedia API <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://neuronpedia.org/api-doc" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://neuronpedia.org/api-doc</a></span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For feature visualization of SAE latents, our objective is as follows. Given an input activation vector <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, an SAE produces a reconstruction via:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{x}=W_{\text{dec}}\cdot f(W_{\text{enc}}x+b_{\text{enc}})+b_{\text{dec}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>dec</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>enc</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mtext>enc</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mtext>dec</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{x}=W_{\text{dec}}\cdot f(W_{\text{enc}}x+b_{\text{enc}})+b_{\text{dec}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>M</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{M}</annotation></semantics></math> is the sparse activation vector. For a target latent <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, the optimization objective is:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{*}=\arg\max_{x}f_{i}(x)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>x</mi></munder></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{*}=\arg\max_{x}f_{i}(x),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{i}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{i}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the activation magnitude of the <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th latent direction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Prompt Optimization</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the abundance of prompt optimization methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramnath et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, most are not applicable to feature visualization, due to fundamental domain differences. For one, it would be infeasible to use exceedingly expensive techniques, such as those which involve LLM API calls <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, comprehensive tree searches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, or model fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. A successful jailbreak prompt justifies hours of compute because it transfers across contexts, whereas feature visualization must be quick to run for individual latents since each requires individual optimization. For another, approaches that leverage prior knowledge to constrain the search space <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">a priori</span> are inapplicable, given the variety of roles played by different latents. Lastly, since latents are specific to each model, surrogate models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paulus et al., 2025</a>)</cite> or simulation techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> cannot be used. We thus focus on prompt methods which are self-contained, relatively inexpensive, and devoid of prior assumptions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.1 </span>Greedy Coordinate Gradient</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al. (2023)</a></cite> optimizes directly in the discrete input space, by starting with a randomly initialized prompt and iteratively swapping out tokens. A gradient-based estimate technique, first introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ebrahimi et al. (2018)</a></cite>, is used to constrain the token search space. The estimate is computed by determining the gradient with respect to a one-hot representation of the input prompt. This is possible due to the equivalence between the regular embedding procedure, in which an embedding matrix <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{E}</annotation></semantics></math> is indexed at the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>th position, where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> is the token index, and a matrix multiplication <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}W_{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}W_{E}</annotation></semantics></math>, between the one-hot vector <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and the embedding matrix. Whereas indexing is non-differentiable, the multiplication procedure allows the gradient of the one-hot vector to be computed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Starting from an initial prompt, GCG computes an estimate by converting the prompt into a <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{prompt\_length}\times\mathrm{vocab\_dim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>prompt</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>length</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>vocab</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>dim</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{prompt\_length}\times\mathrm{vocab\_dim}</annotation></semantics></math> matrix of one-hot vectors and running a backward pass to compute the one-hot gradients as described above. Afterwards, a random position is selected for mutation, and replacements are randomly sampled from the set of <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> lowest gradient prompts to generate <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> candidate prompts. The operative assumption is that the gradient value at a given index is predictive of the loss impact of discretely swapping in the associated token. Lastly, a forward pass is computed to determine the loss for each candidate, and the best performing one is retained. This procedure is repeated until a specified number iterations is reached.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.2 </span>Beam Search</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An alternative way to get around the problems posed by input discreteness is to conduct a gradient-free tree-search over prompt space. However, given the size of typical vocabularies, the search space is prohibitively large. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sadasivan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> propose Beam Search-Based Adversarial Attack (BEAST), which explores prompt space via beam-search, where new candidates are generated by right-appending tokens sampled from the model’s own predicted sequence probabilities. BEAST assumes a complex input structure and optimization objective which are not relevant for our purposes, but at its core it amounts to a simple beam-search procedure. At each step, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> prompt sequences are maintained in a beam. For each sequence, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> candidates are generated by sampling and appending one token via top-k sampling. The <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> lowest loss candidates are then selected for the next beam.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">BEAST’s main advantage is its speed, requiring only forward passes. It thus avoids the overhead of gradient calculation. Additionally, a single forward pass serves dual purposes: evaluating candidate scores and computing logits for the next generation step.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.3 </span>Evolutionary Prompt Optimization</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Evolutionary Prompt Optimization (EPO) is an algorithm introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thompson et al. (2024)</a></cite> specifically for feature visualization in LLMs, which extends GCG by incorporating an evolutionary framework to balance fluency and feature activation. Rather than optimizing for a single objective, EPO maintains a population of prompts distributed along a Pareto frontier: a trade-off curve between fluency (i.e. the mean self-cross-entropy of each candidate) and feature activation strength. Each member of the population optimizes for a different weighting between these objectives, allowing EPO to discover diverse prompts ranging from fluent low-activation prompts to disfluent strongly-activating prompts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The combined activation and fluency objective can be expressed as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(t):=f(t)-\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}H(\text{LLM}(t_{\leq i}),t_{i+1})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>λ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>λ</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>LLM</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(t):=f(t)-\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}H(\text{LLM}(t_{\leq i}),t_{i+1}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{*}_{\lambda}=\arg\max_{t}\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(t)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>t</mi></munder></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>λ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{*}_{\lambda}=\arg\max_{t}\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(t),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(t)</annotation></semantics></math> is the target SAE feature activation for prompt <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{LLM}(t_{\leq i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>LLM</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{LLM}(t_{\leq i})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the language model’s predicted probability distribution over next tokens given prefix <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{\leq i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{\leq i}</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the cross-entropy operator; <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> is a weighting parameter controlling the trade-off between latent maximization and fluency; <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of tokens in prompt <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{\leq i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{\leq i}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the prefix of sequence <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> up to (and including) the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th token and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i+1}</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(i+1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(i+1)</annotation></semantics></math>-th token in <math id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The second term computes the average self-cross-entropy of the sequence, which
is equivalent to the negative log-likelihood under the language model. Lower
cross-entropy corresponds to more ‘fluent’ (i.e. higher likelihood) text.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">A few expansions of EPO have been proposed. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thompson and Sklar (2024)</a></cite> extend EPO with 3 additional operations: insertions, logit-swaps, deletions; where the former two sample new tokens from the model’s own predicted sequence probabilities. While these extensions were made for an adversarial context, they are easily transferable to the feature visualization domain.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shabalin et al. (2024)</a></cite> apply EPO to SAE features obtained from the Gemma 2 2B model, and show that it carries over well, producing moderately interpretable prompts that activate the target latents.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Graham et al. (2025)</a></cite> present ContextBench, a benchmark for fluent context modification targeting latent activation and behavior elicitation, and introduce two extensions to EPO. EPO-Assist periodically queries a large language model to generate novel variations of current outputs, which are then incorporated back into the optimization population. EPO-Inpainting identifies tokens with maximum per-token activation, freezes them, and uses a bidirectional diffusion model (LLaDA) to regenerate surrounding tokens, preserving optimization progress while enhancing fluency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p10.1" class="ltx_p">The authors curate 102 features from Gemma 2 2B across three taxonomic axes: activation density (how frequently the feature fires), vocabulary diversity (semantic breadth of activating concepts), and locality (whether activation is concentrated on single tokens or distributed across sequences), and use it to benchmark and validate the developed methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>ADAPT: Adaptive DynAmic Prompt Tuning</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We describe ADAPT’s three main components: beam-search initialization (<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Initialization ‣ 3 ADAPT: Adaptive DynAmic Prompt Tuning ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>), candidate generation via hybrid mutation (<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Candidate Generation ‣ 3 ADAPT: Adaptive DynAmic Prompt Tuning ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>), and diversity-preserving evaluation and selection (<a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Evaluation and Culling ‣ 3 ADAPT: Adaptive DynAmic Prompt Tuning ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Overview</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our proposed method is an extension of GCG which incorporates several elements that overcome limitations we observed when applied to feature visualization. In this section, we present the method’s core architecture, leaving validation of key design decisions to section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>. An illustrative diagram for ADAPT is shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Overview ‣ 3 ADAPT: Adaptive DynAmic Prompt Tuning ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, and code is included in the supplementary materials.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/ADAPT.drawio.svg" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:476/603;" width="476" height="603"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Diagram for ADAPT.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Initialization</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During experiments with GCG, we found that the choice of initialization strongly affected whether a highly activating prompt was successfully found for a given latent. We also noticed that the optimization trajectory resulting from a given initialization was crucial, with prompts optimized in parallel often achieving drastically different final losses (see subsection <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As such, ADAPT initializes via a beam-search procedure, where several beams are maintained and optimized in parallel, foregoing the need to initialize with an arbitrary user-defined or randomly generated input sequence. Starting from a number of single-token sequences, candidates are generated by right-appending likely next tokens, after which point the lowest loss candidates are included in the next iteration’s beam. The number of beams <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n_groups</span>, the number of initial sequences, the beam-size <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k1</annotation></semantics></math>, and the expansion factor <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k2</annotation></semantics></math> are specified by the user.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We observed that the structure of SAE-latent maximization does not lend itself well to sole use of right-append operations, since we take the latent activation magnitude at the last position, which is continuously relocated to that of the right-appended token. As a hypothetical example, for a latent that exclusively fires for the token <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">foo</span>, a right-append-only beam search would converge on the prompt “<math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cdots" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋯</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cdots</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter"> foo foo foo</span>”, whereas a better prompt might be obtained by refining the left-hand context instead. As such, the initialization procedure also performs middle-inserts, by randomly selecting a sequence position and sampling from the model’s own predicted distribution at that position.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Each beam is independent, which means that our initialization is equivalent to a parallel run of more than one beam search procedure, each with its own initial starting set. The aim is to enable better exploration of the search space, decreasing the likelihood of stagnating in suboptimal local minima. The initialization returns the best prompts across all beams and iterations, without losing track of beam provenance, so that no cross-contamination takes place. Since each iteration increases the sequence length, but the initialization returns the best prompts achieved across all iterations, we may start the main optimization loop with prompts of differing lengths, requiring appropriate masking.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Candidate Generation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ADAPT optimizes over an adaptively sized population of prompts, initialized to the best sequences returned by the beam-search initialization. At each iteration and for each prompt, a fixed, user-specified number of candidates is generated via one of two mutation mechanisms: GCG-style swaps, using the aforementioned gradient-based estimate, and logit-swaps, as in EPO. We multinomially sample the next iteration’s operation based on a user-specified probability value, and retain an excess number of candidates in the surviving population if the next operation is a logit-swap, in order to take advantage of the lower computational requirements of the gradient-free logit-swap mutation. Mutation positions are selected either randomly or by sampling from a distribution over sequence positions that biases towards the selection of later positions. Since the initialization may return underlength prompts, we instead perform middle-inserts for logit-swap iterations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Evaluation and Culling</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ADAPT maintains a complex slot management system. First, each prompt has a group ID, carried over from the initialization procedure. No cross-group selection takes place, to avoid rapid convergence on minor variations of the same prompt, thereby aiding in exploration. Not only does this serve to minimize the likelihood of getting prematurely stuck in local minima, but it also provides diverse, independent examples for a single latent. Notwithstanding, the user may define a <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mergepoint</span> after which the selection mechanism defaults to a greedy global selection that disregards group provenance. Second, two types of slots exist. The first are group-specific “guaranteed” slots, which always contain the group’s best scoring prompt across all iterations. The second set comprises “free” slots, which are allocated via global selection of the highest-improvement candidates, where the improvement is measured as the difference between the achieved loss and the previous group best. This dual structure maintains diversity through the guaranteed slots, while allowing high-performing mutations from any group to claim additional representation through the free slots. With that said, we cap each group at twice its proportional share of free slots.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Before the candidate selection phase can occur, each one must be evaluated. Our evaluator begins by running a forward pass on the candidates, storing both the latent activations and the logits. Afterwards, we apply a fluency penalty mechanism. We employ a global sigmoid fluency penalty schedule, which gradually ramps up depending on several parameters. The penalty weight at any given time <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is a function of the maximum penalty weight <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> that was applied, the iteration of steepest increase <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{\text{mid}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mtext>mid</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{\text{mid}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the parameter <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, which controls the steepness of the increase:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{t}=\frac{\lambda_{\text{max}}}{1+\exp(-s\cdot(t-t_{\text{mid}}))}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>mid</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{t}=\frac{\lambda_{\text{max}}}{1+\exp(-s\cdot(t-t_{\text{mid}}))}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The user may also choose a fluency threshold. Prompts with a mean cross-entropy score below this threshold do not incur any fluency penalty, while prompts above this threshold get penalized in proportion to how much their mean self-cross-entropy exceeds it. We allow the user to fully customize the fluency penalty strategy by setting the cross-entropy threshold to 0 (disabling penalty thresholding), or the steepness <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> to 0 (disabling the fluency schedule entirely). We analyze the importance of fluency in Section <a href="#S4.SS3.SSS3" title="4.3.3 The Role of Fluency ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Feature visualization for SAE evinces the strengths and weaknesses of existing techniques, which informed our design decisions in ADAPT. With the experiments presented in this section our objectives were twofold:</p>
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Comparatively evaluating 4 different methods—ADAPT, GCG, BEAST, and EPO—in order to establish the superiority of our method as a whole.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Validating our design decisions through tailored individual experiments. The results illustrate the failure modes of different techniques, putting into question assumptions held in previous work.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first describe implementation details and hyperparameter settings for all evaluated methods (<a href="#S4.SS1.SSS1" title="4.1.1 Implementation details ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1.1</span></a>), then our model and feature selection procedure (<a href="#S4.SS1.SSS2" title="4.1.2 Model and Feature Selection ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1.2</span></a>), and finally the evaluation metrics used for comparison (<a href="#S4.SS1.SSS3" title="4.1.3 Evaluation ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.1 </span>Implementation details</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hyperparameters were set to sensible defaults according to the authors’ own implementations. Individual optimization runs ran in approximately 80s in optimal GPU conditions, for a single NVIDIA A40 48GB GPU setup.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our implementation of GCG optimizes 6 prompts in parallel, with 32 candidates generated at each iteration. The highest achieved activation is reported, unless stated otherwise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">BEAST was run with a beam size of 128 and expansion factor of 32. The beam size is far higher that GCG’s candidate count due to the lower iteration count (10, corresponding to the prompt length), and the absence of backward passes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We took Thompson et al.’s own implementation as the foundation of our implementation of EPO. Identical hyperparameters were set to match GCG’s as far as possible, with a few key differences. The fluency penalty was set to range from 0.1 to 15 across the 6 slots. The prompt lengths were bounded between 8 and 15, because of the algorithm’s use of length-altering mutations. Operation probabilities were set as follows: GCG-swap (0.5), logit-swap (0.2), insert (0.15), and delete (0.15).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">ADAPT was configured with 10 prompts maintained across 3 diversity groups, with 32 candidates generated per iteration. For the beam-based initialization phase a beam size of 30 and an expansion factor of 32 were used. During optimization, GCG-swap and logit-swap operations were applied with equal probability (0.5 each). Each group retained two guaranteed slots; the remaining 4 or 14 slots (depending on iteration type) were allocated competitively. Cross-entropy regularization was applied with a maximum penalty of 3.0. The GCG estimator sampled from the top 512 tokens ranked by gradient magnitude. Target prompt length was fixed at 10 tokens, and optimization ran for 25 iterations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We sought to maintain comparable prompt lengths across all methods, despite EPO’s variable length implementation. Further details are available in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.2 </span>Model and Feature Selection</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments were performed on Gemma 2 2B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemma Team, 2024</a>)</cite>, in keeping with previous work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shabalin et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. We used the 16k-wide residual stream SAE suite from Gemma Scope <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lieberum et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. The residual stream represents the cumulative computation accessible to all downstream layers, making it the natural target for understanding what information the model maintains and routes through its depth.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A cursory glance at any set of dataset examples for different latents will reveal that they vary widely in their activation patterns and roles. While some activate for specific tokens, others respond to a wide range of tokens that share some functional or semantic role. Some latents are active for longer subsequences, or activate more frequently than others. Accordingly, we designed our latent selection to capture variance along these axes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We curated three latent sets of differing sizes. The larger latent set contains 486 latents sampled from 6 evenly spaced layers (layers 3, 7, 11, 17, 21, and 25) across the model’s 26-layer depth. We began by classifying the first 1000 latents for each layer according to the the items in the taxonomy described by Graham et al.—locality (the narrowness of the range of tokens the latent is active for in the context), diversity (how many different tokens achieve maximal activation across several examples), and density (how frequently the latent activates in the whole dataset). We implemented computational proxies for these items by leveraging information available via the Neuronpedia API; our procedure is detailed in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Latent Selection Procedure ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>. Subsequently, we performed stratified sampling, considering the first 1000 latent directions for each SAE, by applying a <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\times 3\times 3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times 3\times 3</annotation></semantics></math> percentile grid based on the density, locality, and diversity scores. We sampled 4 features from each bin, yielding a total of 81 per layer.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.3 </span>Evaluation</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite EPO’s and ADAPT’s use of fluency penalties, we consider the raw activation values in our metrics, relegating our discussion of fluency to section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>. Since activation magnitudes differ from latent to latent, and also tend to vary across layers—typically, later layers contain latents with much higher Maximally Activating Examples (MAEs), as seen in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1.3 Evaluation ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>—our metrics compare the optimized prompt’s activation with the corresponding MAEs in two ways. The first metric is the <span id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">activation ratio</span>: the ratio between the optimized prompt and the top MAE. The second metric is the <span id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">activation rank</span>, which corresponds to the position the optimized prompt would occupy if ranked among the top 15 de-duplicated MAEs. A prompt with a rank of 1 outperforms all MAEs and, consequently, its activation ratio is greater than 1, while a prompt with rank 16 is worse than all 15 MAEs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/max_activation_by_layer.svg" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/157;" width="476" height="157"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Distribution of top dataset activations for latents 0–49 (by Neuronpedia index) across all layers of Gemma 2 2B.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Overall Performance</h3>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/activation_ratio.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:333/333;" width="333" height="333"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Mean activation ratio (the optimized prompt’s activation divided by the maximally activating dataset example) per layer, for all 4 methods under study.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Row beats column comparison for all 4 methods, considering all 486 latents.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Overall Performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the mean activation ratio per considered layer and for all methods, showing that ADAPT outperforms or is on par with every other method on all layers. Among the previous methods, GCG is dominant for the first layers, while BEAST edges it out on the last layers, indicating a degrading performance profile for GCG toward later layers. Furthermore, the failure modes of GCG and BEAST appear to be complementary, which is corroborated by the fact that ADAPT, which incorporates both a beam-search procedure and gradient-based mutations, achieves a more constant performance profile throughout the layers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The comparison in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Overall Performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows that ADAPT achieves higher activation than GCG on 70.4% of features (Wilcoxon signed-rank <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;10^{-28}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>28</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;10^{-28}</annotation></semantics></math>), further corroborating the improved performance profile.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">EPO underperforms throughout, despite the complexity of its design. This is to be expected to a certain extent, since EPO employs a global selection mechanism which rapidly converges on minor variations of the same prompt spanning the pareto frontier between activation and fluency, whereas our implementation of GCG devotes the computational budget to optimizing 6 prompts independently. In other words, EPO can be seen as an analogue to a single-slot GCG optimization procedure which devotes additional resources to exploring fluent variations which may not vary significantly among themselves, which we are then comparing to the maximum GCG activation across 6 independently-optimized prompts. While this does not undermine the overall approach, it is underpinned by an assumption about the importance of fluency, which we separately revisit in a later section. Since it is the only design element EPO exclusively contains, we forego further analysis of EPO in this section.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<div id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:169.1pt;"><img src="2602.17867v1/rank_matrix_gcg_beast.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:234/231;" width="234" height="231" alt="Refer to caption">

</div></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

<p id="S4.F4.4.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.F4.4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">GCG vs ADAPT</span></p>
</div></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparative ranking matrices
for GCG-ADAPT and GCG-BEAST comparisons.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure">

</div></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
