<p id="S4.F5.4.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.F5.4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">GCG vs ADAPT</span></p>
</div></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Quadrant success per layer for GCG-BEAST and GCG-ADAPT comparisons.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Overall Performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows two activation rank confusion matrices for the GCG-BEAST and GCG-ADAPT comparisons. Arbitrarily considering that a rank greater than 5 corresponds to a successful optimization, the green and red quadrants indicate joint success and failure, respectively, while the other quadrants indicate asymmetric success. The stacked bar charts in Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 Overall Performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> indicate the per-layer share of successful vs. unsuccessful features. The GCG-BEAST comparison further indicates that their failure modes are complementary, with a significant share of GCG-only successes toward earlier layers. The GCG-ADAPT comparison shows that the share of GCG-only successes is marginal, while ADAPT-only successes are substantial, further establishing the superiority of the method.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Validation Experiments</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The overall performance results indicate that the domain is challenging for existing methods. While the target loss function is continuous, a successful optimization run should ideally find the pattern encoded by the latent, which, given the SAE reconstruction objective, is expected to be discrete and monosemantic. For particularly local and low-density features, this pattern might consist of a single vocabulary token, lending a ”needle-in-a-haystack” quality to the task. Additionally, latents are, by definition, non-orthogonal, which means that there can be interference between them, especially for prompts eliciting lower activation magnitudes. In this section, we analyze the effectiveness of existing techniques at finding the key feature patterns, as well as the relationship between our metrics and human interpretability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In order to do so, we curate two smaller latent sets, each with 50 latents sampled from the larger dataset, so as to facilitate targeted experiments. The first is a “balanced” latent set, where we sample features from every layer, seeking to maintain a representative difficulty profile. The second is a “hardness-weighted” latent set, for which we sample 50 features from the last 3 layers, which contain harder latents to optimize (for GCG, specifically), and skew our selection towards more difficult latents.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In order to assess hardness, we determine the inverse of the average activation ratio obtained by GCG for every iteration, averaged across all 6 prompts. The average activation ratio is equivalent to the ratio between the area under the trajectory curve and the area below <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=a_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=a_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> being the maximal dataset activation. Intuitively, an easy latent is one for which GCG rapidly converges on a solution that is equal to or greater than <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> across all 6 slots, in which case the AUC ratio will be 1 or lower. If all trajectories plateau below the dataset reference maximum, then the hardness will be far greater than 1. The hardness <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> for a latent <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> is given by:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{l}=\left(\frac{1}{S\cdot a_{\max}\cdot T}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\max(L_{s}^{(t)},0)\right)^{-1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>S</mi></munderover><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{l}=\left(\frac{1}{S\cdot a_{\max}\cdot T}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\max(L_{s}^{(t)},0)\right)^{-1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of prompt slots, <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of iterations, and <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{s}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{s}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the loss (negative activation) for slot <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> at iteration <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We divided latents into 5 hardness quintiles based on percentile boundaries, and sampled features from each quintile according to two strategies. The uniform sample drew 10 features from each quintile (50 total), while the hardness-weighted sample emphasized harder features with counts of (5, 8, 10, 12, 15) from the easiest to the hardest quintiles, respectively (50 total).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.1 </span>The GCG estimate’s signal-to-noise ratio</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The gradient-based estimate used in GCG (henceforth, the ‘GCG estimate’) is predicated on the assumption that the loss impact of discretely including each token is well-approximated by its corresponding gradient computed for the one-hot encoding. If the GCG estimate were a perfect approximation, we would expect low-ranked tokens—the tokens with the most negative gradient—to lead to the greatest loss decreases. Conversely, we would also expect the tokens resulting in the largest loss decreases to have the lowest gradients.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In order to assess these two claims, we perform the following experiment on the balanced latent set. For each latent, we begin by determining the two slots which achieved the highest and lowest final activation, respectively. For each slot, we obtain the cached prompt trajectory from the main run. Afterwards, we generate 128 new candidate mutations in two ways. The first 64 are generated via the same GCG estimate procedure as in the original GCG, with a top-<math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> of 1024 (doubling the candidate count and top-<math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>). The last 64 are generated by instead performing top-<math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> sampling from the model’s own probabilities, with <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.95</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.95</annotation></semantics></math>. We keep track of all the generated candidates which constitute improvements over the cached prompt’s activation. We also fix the trajectory to ensure comparable results between the two candidate generation methods.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F7.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:165.6pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/gcg_improvement_counts.svg" id="S4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/164;" width="229" height="164"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F7.fig1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.F7.fig1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Number of improvements per estimate rank bin.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F7.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:165.6pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/gcg_improvement_mass.svg" id="S4.F7.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/164;" width="229" height="164"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F7.fig2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S4.F7.fig2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Improvement mass per estimate rank bin.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.3.1 The GCG estimate’s signal-to-noise ratio ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows that the gradient rank distribution for improvements obtained via GCG is quite close to uniform, indicating that lower gradient values do not yield remarkably more improvements. Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.3.1 The GCG estimate’s signal-to-noise ratio ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, on the other hand, shows that the distribution of the sum of improvements is more uneven, with the lower gradient bins containing a disproportionate share of the absolute improvements. This suggests that, while the GCG estimate is noisy, and a large share of the sampled candidates are only marginally better than would otherwise be expected, it is able to occasionally yield disproportionately good candidates among its highest ranks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F9" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F9.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:165.6pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/logit_gradient_ranks.svg" id="S4.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/165;" width="229" height="165"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F9.fig1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="S4.F9.fig1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">GCG estimate rank distribution for improvement candidates obtained via the logit-swap procedure.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F9.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:165.6pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/random_gradient_ranks.svg" id="S4.F9.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/165;" width="229" height="165"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F9.fig2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="S4.F9.fig2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">GCG-Estimate rank distribution for improvement candidates obtained via the random sampling procedure.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 4.3.1 The GCG estimate’s signal-to-noise ratio ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> shows the gradient rank distribution for candidates selected via gradient-free logit sampling. While the lowest gradient bins capture a disproportionate share of the improvements, the distribution is close to uniform for the middle bins, indicating that there are many improvements which the GCG estimate fails to attribute an appropriate gradient to. Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 4.3.1 The GCG estimate’s signal-to-noise ratio ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> further illustrates this, showing the distribution of the gradient ranks of tokens sampled uniformly from the entire vocabulary, with lower-gradient ranges containing more improvements. The bimodal distribution for the logit-swap candidates nonetheless suggests an interesting relationship between predicted probabilities and the biases of the GCG estimate. Specifically, the GCG estimate appears to be biased towards certain commonly occurring tokens more than would be expected by chance, while systematically undervaluing certain tokens, even when they bring about loss decreases. Inspecting the sampled tokens from the last bins, we found that they mostly correspond to punctuation and formatting tokens.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.2 </span>Consistency of GCG</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While the experiments in Subsection <a href="#S4.SS3.SSS1" title="4.3.1 The GCG estimate’s signal-to-noise ratio ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3.1</span></a> establish the poor signal-to-noise ratio of GCG, with many good candidates being underestimated, and many highly estimated candidates underperforming, questions remain as to how reliably GCG can converge on high activation regions of prompt space. For this reason, we now analyze how sensitive GCG is to initialization and trajectory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the benchmark in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Overall Performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, GCG was configured to optimize six prompts in parallel. We observed a good deal of inter-slot variability in final activation. In this subsection, we consider the impact of initialization on the performance of GCG, by answering two questions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Do some specific initial prompts reliably predict higher final activations?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Does GCG consistently attain similar activations across different runs initialized with the same prompt?</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To answer these questions, we conduct a simple experiment. We begin by determining which of the 6 initial prompts in the main benchmark achieved the both the highest and lowest average final activations. Since the highest-performing prompt was obtained through autoregressive generation, and the lowest-performing prompt consists of randomly sampled tokens from the vocabulary, we call them the “autoregressive” and “random” prompts, respectively. Afterwards, we conduct a benchmark on the hardness-weighted latent set, where 3 of the 6 initial slots are initialized with the autoregressive prompt, and the remaining 3 are initialized with the random prompt.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F11" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F11.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:165.6pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/intra_prompt_variability.svg" id="S4.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/168;" width="229" height="168"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F11.fig1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 10</span>: </span><span id="S4.F11.fig1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Distribution of activation variability across runs from identical initializations, normalized by the MAE.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F11.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:165.6pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/inter_prompt_variability.svg" id="S4.F11.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:229/225;" width="229" height="225"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F11.fig2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 11</span>: </span><span id="S4.F11.fig2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of best activations achieved from autoregressive versus random initializations. Points above diagonal indicate autoregressive advantage.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 4.3.2 Consistency of GCG ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> shows the intra-prompt distribution of final activation ranges, normalized by the maximal dataset activation. It is clear that for both prompts there is significant variability, meaning that the same initialization can yield very different results depending on the trajectory, which is selected stochastically. This indicates that GCG is prone to falling in local minima depending on the specific trajectory through prompt space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 4.3.2 Consistency of GCG ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> shows the comparison between the performance for both slots across all slots, with the mean and max normalized activations, respectively, in each plot. It illustrates the inter-prompt variability by establishing that the autoregressive prompt slots consistently obtain higher activations than the random prompt.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, these results establish that GCG’s performance is heavily dependent on location in prompt space. In other words, for some starting locations, GCG is significantly more likely to converge on high-activating token patterns, although the greedy candidate selection often produces trajectories that evolve towards local minima, highlighting the importance of open-ended exploration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 4.3.2 Consistency of GCG ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> shows the distribution of activation ranges across runs from identical initializations, normalized by maximal dataset activation. The median variability of 0.20 indicates that runs from the same starting point can diverge substantially, suggesting GCG is prone to converging on different local minima depending on the stochastically-selected trajectory through prompt space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 4.3.2 Consistency of GCG ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> compares best activations achieved from autoregressive versus random initializations. Autoregressive initialization outperforms random initialization in 62% of configurations, demonstrating that the starting location in prompt space meaningfully influences optimization outcomes, but does not fully predict them.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, these results establish that GCG’s performance depends heavily on both initialization and trajectory. While autoregressive initialization provides a consistent advantage, the substantial intra-prompt variability highlights the importance of maintaining diverse exploration to avoid local minima.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.3 </span>The Role of Fluency</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GCG usually produces ‘gibberish’ prompts, which contain incoherent token sequences mixing languages, scripts, punctuation, and subword fragments. This is due to the lack of any constraint on possible token sequences. In the adversarial domain, fluency is usually enforced to bypass perplexity-based filters and to obtain in-distribution prompts. However, it is not immediately apparent that the same desiderata apply to feature visualization. For one, perplexity filters have no analogue in this domain; for another, adversarial behavioral objectives admit multiple sufficient mechanisms (e.g. simultaneously suppressing refusal directions and hijacking attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>), whereas targeted latent activation objectives specify the intervention site directly, achieving mechanistic specificity by construction rather than requiring auxiliary constraints.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given the attributes of the feature visualization domain, two putative roles for fluency are relevant:</p>
<ul id="S4.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Regularization:</span> preventing optimization from getting stuck in local minima, resulting in the return of low activation prompts.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Interpretability:</span> preventing high activation solutions that are uninterpretable or unrelated to the feature pattern <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thompson et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F12" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/fluency_activation_ratio.svg" id="S4.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/262;" width="381" height="262"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F12.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 12</span>: </span><span id="S4.F12.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Activation ratio distribution for GCG runs with varying fluency penalty weights.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The first hypothesis suggests that a fluency penalty may reshape the loss landscape, smoothing over narrow valleys and sharp local minima that trap optimization in gibberish regions. To test this, we rerun GCG on the hardness-weighted latent set with an added self-cross-entropy penalty:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(t)=-f(t)+\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}H(\text{LLM}(t_{\leq i}),t_{i+1})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>λ</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>LLM</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(t)=-f(t)+\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}H(\text{LLM}(t_{\leq i}),t_{i+1}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(t)</annotation></semantics></math> is the target latent activation, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the cross-entropy, and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda\in\{0.3,1.0,3.0,9.0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3.0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9.0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda\in\{0.3,1.0,3.0,9.0\}</annotation></semantics></math> controls the fluency-activation tradeoff.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ 4.3.3 The Role of Fluency ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> shows that higher values of <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> hinder optimization across the whole latent set, thereby undermining the hypothesis. Notwithstanding, we highlight that this experiment does not directly bear on the fluency configuration used in the ADAPT benchmark, since higher penalties are only applied in later iterations, leaving the initialization and early optimization periods relatively unhindered by fluency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To assess whether fluency penalties improve interpretability and to validate ADAPT’s design, we conducted a manual evaluation comparing three conditions: GCG, GCG with a fluency penalty (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>), and ADAPT. Three raters (including one author) evaluated prompts on 60 latents: the 50-latent hardness-weighted set plus 10 additional latents with activation ratio greater than 1.0, included to better probe whether high-activation prompts recover interpretable patterns. For each latent, raters viewed the latent’s explanation, maximally activating dataset examples, and three prompts (one per condition, order randomized). Since the patterns captured by certain latents can be hard to infer, consisting of upweighted predictions which are not necessarily borne out in the dataset examples, structural properties of the text, or otherwise unintuitive patterns, the explanations were generated by the authors, although a set of maximally activating examples was provided<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              We have included the annotation file in the supplementary materials.</span></span></span>. Prompts were rated on a 1–5 scale: (1) no discernible pattern, (2) semantic ballpark but not discernible, (3) pattern understandable but not evident from prompt alone, (4) pattern present but differs from examples (e.g., different language), (5) pattern obvious and matches examples. We computed Krippendorff’s <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> for inter-rater agreement, obtaining <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.650" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.650</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.650</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F13" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/rating_vs_ratio_matrix.svg" id="S4.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/132;" width="476" height="132"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F13.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 13</span>: </span><span id="S4.F13.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Rank/rating co-occurrence matrix for GCG, GCG with a <math id="S4.F13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=1.0</annotation></semantics></math> fluency penalty, and ADAPT, respectively.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F14" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/rating_histogram_by_method.svg" id="S4.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/132;" width="476" height="132"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F14.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 14</span>: </span><span id="S4.F14.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Rating distribution for GCG, GCG with a <math id="S4.F14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=1.0</annotation></semantics></math> fluency penalty, and ADAPT, respectively.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ 4.3.3 The Role of Fluency ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> shows that, for GCG, higher activation reliably correlates (Pearson <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.645,p&lt;10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.645</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.645,p&lt;10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>) with more interpretable prompts, despite the lack of fluency constraints. Indeed, high activation (ratio<math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;1.0</annotation></semantics></math>) prompts seem overwhelmingly interpretable, whereas the correlation is less clear for lower activation regimes. The <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=1.0</annotation></semantics></math> run shows similar patterns, with no remarkable improvement in interpretability. Indeed, as Figure <a href="#S4.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ 4.3.3 The Role of Fluency ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> shows, the interpretability distribution is remarkably similar between the two methods, with the penalty appearing to slightly compress the rating distribution rather than shift it toward higher interpretability.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F15" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17867v1/mean_rating_by_method.svg" id="S4.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/261;" width="381" height="261"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F15.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 15</span>: </span><span id="S4.F15.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Quality rating for each method averaged over all latents and annotators.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our analysis also establishes that ADAPT is significantly better at generating interpretable prompts. Figure <a href="#S4.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ 4.3.3 The Role of Fluency ‣ 4.3 Validation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> shows the mean rating for each of the methods, establishing the superiority of ADAPT (Wilcoxon Statistic of <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4459.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4459.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4459.5</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;10^{-8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;10^{-8}</annotation></semantics></math>), while showing that GCG with <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=1.0</annotation></semantics></math> does not produce significant changes in human-rated interpretability. Lastly, we note that because the activation ratio is a mere proxy for human interpretability, these results provide the most compelling evidence in support of our design decisions in ADAPT.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Extensions</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ADAPT naturally extends to objectives involving multiple latents by summing their activations. We conducted a brief experiment with dual latent optimization to illustrate this extension potential. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shabalin et al. (2024)</a></cite>, we optimize dual-latent objectives using an <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{0.1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>0.1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{0.1}</annotation></semantics></math> norm, which encourages balanced activation of both latents rather than maximizing one at the expense of the other:</p>
<table id="S5.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(t)=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}f_{i}(t)\\
f_{j}(t)\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{0.1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mtable displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>0.1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(t)=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}f_{i}(t)\\
f_{j}(t)\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{0.1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{i}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{i}(t)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{j}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{j}(t)</annotation></semantics></math> are the activation magnitudes of the two target latents for prompt <math id="S5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We found not all pairs of latents are amenable to optimization, since their associated patterns can be mutually exclusive. For instance, if both are high in locality (firing for narrow subsequences), it might not be possible to obtain high simultaneous activations on the same position. Notwithstanding, we achieved success in jointly optimizing pairs where one latent was local and the other fired for wide contexts. Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5 Extensions ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows combinations of 3 different layer 25 residual stream latents, and their respective optimized prompts. Latent <a href="https://www.neuronpedia.org/gemma-2-2b/25-gemmascope-res-16k/823" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">823</a> is a low locality latent which fires for contexts related to the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Latent <a href="https://www.neuronpedia.org/gemma-2-2b/25-gemmascope-res-16k/2738" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">2738</a> is highly local and activates for terms like “bit” and “little”. Latent <a href="https://www.neuronpedia.org/gemma-2-2b/25-gemmascope-res-16k/1264" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">1264</a> is local and fires for the token “syn” and spelling variants. Lastly, latent <a href="https://www.neuronpedia.org/gemma-2-2b/25-gemmascope-res-16k/154" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">154</a> is low locality and is active for text describing magnets and their properties. ADAPT is able to find interesting combinations of the patterns encoded by each latent which are interpretable, most notably the last example where the subsequence “Stark magnet” concisely fits the MCU (Tony Stark) and magnet patterns.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Optimized prompts for dual-latent objectives. All latents from layer 25. Prompts successfully activate both target latents, with local features (2738, 1264) appearing as specific tokens and low-locality features (823, 154) reflected in semantic context.</figcaption>

<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The results presented here suggest that extending ADAPT to visualization of circuits or other complex objectives would prove fruitful, though we leave this to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented ADAPT, a hybrid prompt optimization method for LLM feature visualization. Through evaluation on SAE latents from Gemma 2 2B, we identified key failure modes of existing methods: GCG’s gradient-based estimates exhibit poor signal-to-noise ratios and high sensitivity to initialization, while gradient-free beam search provides complementary exploration capabilities but lacks the fine-grained refinement needed for convergence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">ADAPT addresses these limitations through three principal design choices: (1) beam-search initialization to start optimization in favorable regions of prompt space, (2) adaptive mixing of gradient-guided and logit-based mutations to balance exploitation with exploration, and (3) a diversity-preserving slot management system that maintains independent optimization trajectories to avoid premature convergence to local minima.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments demonstrate that ADAPT outperforms GCG on 70.4% of features (<math id="S6.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;10^{-28}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>28</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;10^{-28}</annotation></semantics></math>) and achieves consistently strong performance across all model layers, unlike prior methods whose effectiveness varies with depth. Importantly, our manual evaluation reveals that high activation correlates strongly with human-rated interpretability (<math id="S6.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.645" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.645</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.645</annotation></semantics></math>), and that ADAPT produces significantly more interpretable prompts than baselines, providing direct evidence that optimizing for activation recovers meaningful feature patterns rather than exploiting artifacts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">These results establish that feature visualization for LLMs is tractable, but requires design assumptions tailored to the domain’s unique challenges: discrete optimization over a vast token space, interference between non-orthogonal latent directions, and a loss landscape prone to local minima. We hope ADAPT provides a useful tool for interpretability research, and welcome extensions for visualization of steering vectors, circuit components, and other latent directions where exhaustive dataset search is prohibitive.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Limitations and Future Work.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluation focused on residual stream SAEs from a single model family. Extending ADAPT to larger models and more diverse latent extraction methods remains as possible future work. Additionally, while our metrics provide rigorous comparison, integration with automated interpretability pipelines that correlate with human judgment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paulo and Belrose, 2025</a>)</cite> would enable larger-scale evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

               <math id="alg1.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\textsc{GradientMutate}(\mathcal{P},\nabla)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">GradientMutate</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>∇</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\textsc{GradientMutate}(\mathcal{P},\nabla)</annotation></semantics></math> {Low-gradient tokens}

</div>
<div id="alg1.l7" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">7:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">else</span>


</div>
<div id="alg1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">8:</span></span>
              
              
               <math id="alg1.l8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\textsc{LogitMutate}(\mathcal{P})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">LogitMutate</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\textsc{LogitMutate}(\mathcal{P})</annotation></semantics></math> {Model’s predictions}

</div>
<div id="alg1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l9.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">9:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">if</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l10" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l10.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">10:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> each candidate <math id="alg1.l10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\in\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c\in\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l10.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>



</div>
<div id="alg1.l11" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l11.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">11:</span></span>
              
              
               <math id="alg1.l11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{c}\leftarrow f(c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{c}\leftarrow f(c)</annotation></semantics></math>;  <math id="alg1.l11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{i}\leftarrow\lambda_{\max}/(1+e^{-s(i-t_{\text{mid}})})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mtext>mid</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{i}\leftarrow\lambda_{\max}/(1+e^{-s(i-t_{\text{mid}})})</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l12" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l12.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">12:</span></span>
              
              
               <math id="alg1.l12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{score}_{c}\leftarrow a_{c}-\lambda_{i}\cdot\max(0,\text{CE}(c)-\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mtext>score</mtext><mi>c</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>CE</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{score}_{c}\leftarrow a_{c}-\lambda_{i}\cdot\max(0,\text{CE}(c)-\tau)</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l13" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l13.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">13:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l13.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l13.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l14" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l14.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">14:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l14.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <math id="alg1.l14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=1</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l14.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">to</span> <math id="alg1.l14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l14.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>



</div>
<div id="alg1.l15" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l15.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">15:</span></span>
              
              
               Keep top candidates from group <math id="alg1.l15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> in guaranteed slots

</div>
<div id="alg1.l16" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l16.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">16:</span></span>
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l16.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l16.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l17" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l17.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">17:</span></span>
              
              
              Fill remaining slots globally by score (with per-group cap)

</div>
<div id="alg1.l18" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l18.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">18:</span></span>
              
              
              <math id="alg1.l18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}\leftarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}\leftarrow</annotation></semantics></math> selected candidates

</div>
<div id="alg1.l19" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l19.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">19:</span></span>
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l19.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l19.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l20" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l20.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">20:</span></span>
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l20.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">return</span>  <math id="alg1.l20.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\arg\max_{t\in\mathcal{P}}f(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arg\max_{t\in\mathcal{P}}f(t)</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
</div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Latent Selection Procedure</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We computed proxies for the three taxonomic axes described by Graham et al. using data available via the Neuronpedia API.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Density.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A latent’s density corresponds to the frequency with which it activates. We take the fraction of tokens for which the latent is active, which is directly provided by the Neuronpedia API as <span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">frac_nonzero</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Locality.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Locality describes how concentrated a latent’s activation is within a sequence. A highly local latent exhibits high activation for a single token with negligible activation for surrounding tokens, whereas a low-locality latent may activate across entire phrases. Given a set of <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> maximally activating examples for a latent, let <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{(j)}=(a^{(j)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(j)}_{L_{j}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{(j)}=(a^{(j)}_{1},\ldots,a^{(j)}_{L_{j}})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the activation values across all <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> tokens in example <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>. We define locality as:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Locality}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\max_{i}a^{(j)}_{i}}{\sum_{i}a^{(j)}_{i}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Locality</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Locality}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\max_{i}a^{(j)}_{i}}{\sum_{i}a^{(j)}_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">For a highly local latent, this ratio approaches 1, as the maximally activating token captures most of the activation mass.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Diversity.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diversity indicates the variety of tokens a latent responds to. A low-diversity latent fires for a specific token, while a high-diversity latent activates for many different tokens sharing a semantic or functional role. Given the top <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> maximally activating examples, let <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{N}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{N}\}</annotation></semantics></math> be the set of tokens achieving maximal activation in each example. We define diversity as:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Diversity}=\frac{|\text{lowercase}(T)|}{N}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Diversity</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mtext>lowercase</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Diversity}=\frac{|\text{lowercase}(T)|}{N}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{lowercase}(T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>lowercase</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{lowercase}(T)</annotation></semantics></math> applies lowercasing to all tokens before computing the unique set size. This normalization accounts for capitalization variants of the same underlying token.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Human Evaluation Protocol</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Annotators were presented with the following information for each latent: (1) an explanation of what the latent detects, (2) maximally activating dataset examples with highlighted tokens showing activation strength, and (3) three generated prompts from different methods in randomized order, with the 3 most likely token completions in square brackets to aid in rating ‘Say X’ features. Annotators could also access interactive exploration via Neuronpedia. Figure <a href="#A1.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ A.3 Human Evaluation Protocol ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> shows a single latent’s annotation interface.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Prompts were rated on the following 1–5 scale:</p>
<ol id="A1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No discernible pattern</span>: The prompt appears random or unrelated to the latent’s function.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Semantic ballpark</span>: The prompt is in the general semantic area of the reference examples but is otherwise uninterpretable.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pattern understandable</span>: The pattern the prompt is targeting is understandable given context, but not discernible from the optimized prompt alone.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pattern present but different</span>: The pattern is clearly present but differs in some way from reference examples (e.g., different language, domain, or format).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">5.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pattern obvious and matches</span>: The pattern is immediately obvious and closely matches the maximally activating dataset examples.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F16" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17867v1/images/annotation_example.png" id="A1.F16.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/406;" width="476" height="406" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F16.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 16</span>: </span><span id="A1.F16.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Annotation task example for the ‘magnet’ latent.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>

    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
